hints: Focus on oxidation numbers rather than just atoms, redox is all about change in oxidation number.
Work out the oxidation number of Cl in $\text{ClO}_2$, $\text{ClO}_2^-$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$, remembering O is -2.
Check if oxygen changes at all, then see if the same element both goes up and goes down in oxidation number.
walkthrough:
**Find the oxidation number of chlorine everywhere**

Think of oxidation number as the score for each atom. Oxygen is almost always -2, so we can solve for chlorine.

$$\text{In ClO}_2: x + 2(-2) = 0 \text{ so } x = +4$$
$$\text{In ClO}_2^-: x + 2(-2) = -1 \text{ so } x = +3$$
$$\text{In ClO}_3^-: x + 3(-2) = -1 \text{ so } x = +5$$

**Check the oxidation number of oxygen everywhere**

Oxygen starts at -2 in $\text{ClO}_2$ and in $\text{OH}^-$. It ends at -2 in $\text{ClO}_2^-$, $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

$$\text{O: } -2 \rightarrow -2 \text{ (no change)}$$

**Decide who is oxidised and who is reduced**

One Cl goes from +4 to +3. That is a decrease, so gain of electrons, so reduction. The other Cl goes from +4 to +5. That is an increase, so loss of electrons, so oxidation.

This is a classic disproportionation, where the same element is both oxidised and reduced.

options.A: Incorrect. Chlorine is involved in both oxidation and reduction, not just oxidation. Oxygen shows no change in oxidation number (-2 throughout), so it is neither oxidised nor reduced.
options.B: Incorrect. Chlorine is involved in both reduction (+4 to +3) and oxidation (+4 to +5), not just reduction. Oxygen stays at -2 on both sides, so it is not oxidised.
options.C: Correct. One Cl atom goes +4 to +3 (reduced to $\text{ClO}_2^-$) and the other Cl atom goes +4 to +5 (oxidised to $\text{ClO}_3^-$). This is disproportionation of chlorine.
options.D: Incorrect. All oxygen atoms remain at oxidation number -2 in reactants ($\text{ClO}_2$, $\text{OH}^-$) and products ($\text{ClO}_2^-$, $\text{ClO}_3^-$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). No oxygen is oxidised or reduced.
